evidence: Prop. 1.2.14: volucrēs nūllā dulcius arte canant (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of birds, and of frogs too, canere is the usual word; of a cock it is “crow”.

terms.grammar: intransitive; the dative of the one sung along with
terms.comment: Of voices or instruments sounding together; Suetonius uses it of Caligula singing along with a tragic actor in the theatre.

phrases.latin: St! Audīn'? Avis in arbore canit.
phrases.english: Shh! Do you hear? A bird is singing in the tree.
the birds make their plaint in the woods

phrases.latin: et mātūtīnī volucrum sub culmine cantūs
phrases.english: and the birds’ morning songs under the eaves

phrases.latin: Nōstī hoc carmen? Ūnā mēcum cane.
phrases.english: Do you know this song? Sing along with me.

phrases.latin: canendī ac saltandī voluptāte ita efferēbātur, ut nē pūblicīs quidem spectāculīs temperāret quō minus et tragoedō prōnūntiantī concineret
phrases.english: he was so carried away by the pleasure of singing and dancing that not even at the public shows could he stop himself from singing along with the tragic actor as he delivered his lines
Let’s sing something while we walk.

phrases.latin: cantantēs licet ūsque (minus via laedit) eāmus
phrases.english: let’s go singing all the way (the road hurts less)

sources: Lewis & Short: canto · Lewis & Short: concino
